title: Qatar | QCB Technology Risks, Cybersecurity and Data Protection
tagline: Qatar Central Bank's technology risk, data protection and cloud rules in practice: awareness, the 1-hour incident report, breaches, continuity and cloud.
sectors: Conventional banks licensed by the Qatar Central Bank
Business continuity, risk and internal audit
description:
A country-specific quest for staff of **conventional banks licensed and supervised by the Qatar Central Bank (QCB)** outside the Qatar Financial Centre. It is built on the **QCB Technology Risks Regulation for banks (January 2018)**, the **QCB Data Handling and Protection Regulation** and the **QCB Cloud Computing Regulation** (in force from 15 April 2024), with **Law No. 13 of 2016 on Personal Data Privacy Protection** covered in general terms.

The Technology Risks Regulation requires every bank to run a funded security awareness programme: information security training at induction, a refresher at least once a year that teaches staff to spot social engineering, an assessment after training, attendance and acknowledgement records, and training sessions on cyber threats for senior management and the board. All users must be trained to report incidents, and the Data Handling and Protection Regulation adds privacy and data protection training. So this quest is for every employee, with extra depth for managers, IT, data and continuity teams.

You will learn governance, phishing and fraud, data classification, the 1-hour critical incident report, breach handling, continuity and cloud.

This quest builds knowledge of Qatar's framework; it does not replace your institution's own information security, data protection and continuity policies and procedures, which you must always follow.
audience: All employees and long-term contractors of QCB-licensed conventional banks who need induction or annual security awareness training
Branch, contact centre, card and digital banking staff who face phishing, social engineering and fraud attempts
IT, information security and incident response staff who classify, escalate and report incidents to the QCB
Data owners, data stewards and the Data Privacy Officer applying the QCB Data Handling and Protection Regulation
Business continuity, vendor, cloud and risk teams, internal auditors, senior managers and board members
outcomes: Explain how the QCB Technology Risks, Data Handling and Protection and Cloud Computing regulations fit together and who is accountable
Apply the security awareness duties: induction, yearly refresher, social engineering, assessment, records and board training
Recognise and report phishing, social engineering and fraud attempts through the bank's channels
Classify and handle PII, sensitive personal and sensitive financial information, with lawful bases, consent and retention
Escalate incidents so critical ones reach the QCB within 1 hour, and handle data breaches with the QCB, NCSA and Ministry of Interior
Describe the QCB's expectations for business continuity testing, cloud arrangements and the bank's yearly compliance cycle

quest.name: Shield of the Doha Skyline
quest.premise: You have just joined the Information Security Group of Dafna Bank, a fictional conventional bank licensed by the Qatar Central Bank, with its head office in West Bay, Doha, and branches in Al Wakrah and Al Khor. The bank's yearly compliance report to the QCB is due and the awareness programme must be refreshed. With CISO Maryam Al Marri, incident manager Joseph Mwangi, Data Privacy Officer Priya Nair and business continuity head Khalid Al Naimi, clear five stages, then face the final boss: board risk committee chair Ahmed Al Sada.

sessions.title: Qatar's Technology Risk Rulebook: Three QCB Regulations and Who Is Accountable
sessions.summary: How the QCB Technology Risks Regulation, the Data Handling and Protection Regulation and the Cloud Computing Regulation fit together, and what the board, senior management, the CISO and every employee must do.

cards.title: Day one in the Watchtower
cards.setting: Information Security Group, Dafna Bank head office, West Bay, Doha. 8:00 am, Sunday.

lines.text: Your access badge works on the third try. The screen on the wall shows a live map of blocked attacks, and a printed QCB regulation sits on your new desk, already full of coloured tabs.
Welcome to Dafna Bank. I'm Maryam, the CISO. Good timing: our yearly compliance report to Qatar Central Bank is due and the awareness programme needs its annual refresh.
Joseph, incident response. Last night someone in Al Khor clicked a fake parcel link. Nothing was lost, but I need people who know when to call me.
Priya, Data Privacy Officer. And I keep hearing that cyber rules belong to IT. Half of my data questions are about people, not servers.
Exactly why you start here, in the Watchtower. Before any tool, you need the map: which QCB rules apply, who owns what, and what the board must sign.
(passing by) Ahmed Al Sada, board risk committee. Maryam, the committee wants the cyber indicators before our next meeting. Six months goes quickly.
It does. Let's get our new colleague ready to brief you.

cards.title: Qatar's technology risk rulebook in five scenes

scenes.heading: The supervisor
scenes.narration: Qatar Central Bank licenses and supervises banks outside the Qatar Financial Centre. Its Information Security rules set out what every bank must do to manage technology and cyber risk.

scenes.heading: The core regulation
scenes.narration: The Technology Risks Regulation for banks, issued in January 2018, covers governance, people, risk, continuity, IT operations, security controls and fraud. Most of what you do day to day traces back to it.

scenes.heading: The data regulation
scenes.narration: The Data Handling and Protection Regulation covers how all QCB-regulated financial institutions classify, use, keep, share and protect data, including customer consent and data breaches.

scenes.heading: The cloud regulation
scenes.narration: The Cloud Computing Regulation came into force on 15 April 2024. It governs how a regulated entity selects, contracts, monitors and exits cloud services.

scenes.heading: The national law
scenes.narration: Above them sits Qatar's personal data privacy law, Law Number 13 of 2016. The QCB data regulation requires personal data to be processed in line with it.

cards.title: Layers that govern Dafna Bank's technology risk
cards.caption: Each layer must fit the one above it. Where the bank's procedure is silent, the regulation still applies.

items.label: Law No. 13 of 2016
items.detail: Qatar's personal data privacy law, administered nationally by the National Cyber Security Agency

items.label: QCB regulations
items.detail: Technology Risks Regulation (2018), Data Handling and Protection Regulation, Cloud Computing Regulation (2024)

items.label: Board-approved policy
items.detail: Cyber security policy, strategy, budget and risk appetite approved by the board

items.label: Standards and procedures
items.detail: Reviewed at least yearly; acceptable use, classification, incident and continuity procedures

items.label: What you do every day
items.detail: Spot, protect, report: the habits the awareness programme builds

cards.title: Which regulation covers it?
cards.prompt: Match each topic to the QCB text that mainly governs it.

pairs.right: Technology Risks Regulation, section 2.2 on staff competency and training
Data Handling and Protection Regulation, customer data protection section
Technology Risks Regulation, incident management section
Data Handling and Protection Regulation, organisational governance

pairs.left: Four unplanned continuity drills a year
pairs.right: Technology Risks Regulation, business continuity section

cards.question: Which statement best describes how the QCB Data Handling and Protection Regulation relates to Law No. 13 of 2016?
options: It requires personal data to be processed in line with the 2016 law
It replaces the 2016 law for banks in Qatar
It applies only where the 2016 law is silent
It applies only to banks inside the Qatar Financial Centre
cards.explanation: The QCB regulation lists Law No. 13 of 2016 among the laws a financial institution must comply with and says personal data must be processed in line with it. It adds sector rules on top; it does not replace the law. QFC firms follow their own regulator.

cards.title: What the board must own
cards.body:
The Technology Risks Regulation puts cyber risk on the board's agenda, not just IT's. The board (or a board-authorised committee) must:

- **approve** the cyber security function and framework, the **cyber security policy**, and the overall **strategy and budget**, with contingency built in
- **approve a cyber risk appetite**: how much risk the bank will accept
- have **adequate technical representation**, people with real cyber security experience, to guide it
- ask senior management to **review the adequacy of cyber controls at least once a year** and justify any material gaps
- **monitor cyber security indicators at least every six months**, with senior management fixing deviations

The indicators cover risks, compliance, incidents, threat level, key projects and **awareness and culture**, such as learning scores and training coverage. Your training records feed the board pack.

cards.title: Board, CISO or every employee?
cards.prompt: Sort each duty to the person or body the QCB rules give it to.

items.text: Approve the cyber risk appetite
Approve the cyber security strategy and budget
Review cyber indicators at least twice a year
Manage the security awareness programme
Facilitate the security forum meetings
Report suspicious emails to the security team
Complete the yearly awareness refresher
Sign the confidentiality agreement on joining

cards.title: Who does the CISO report to?

lines.text: Question from my team: why doesn't Maryam just report to the CIO? IT and security work together every day.
Working together is essential. Reporting to IT is the problem. Imagine I find that an IT project skipped a security test to hit a deadline.
Then your boss would be the person who missed the test.
That's the conflict the QCB rule removes. The Information Security Group is separate from IT, and the CISO reports to an independent governing body, not to the CIO or CTO.
And the board hears from the Information Security Committee directly, including how the awareness programme is going.

cards.back: Heads the Information Security Group, manages the awareness programme and reports to an independent body, not the IT head.
A separate function focused only on information and cyber security, segregated from the IT division that builds and runs systems.
Senior leaders such as the CEO, CFO, CIO and heads of HR, legal, risk, audit and operations, facilitated by the CISO.
Reviews policies, incidents and the status of the awareness programme, and reports to the board.
Required by the data regulation; advises on privacy and reports to the CEO or most senior manager.
A senior manager designated to lead business continuity, including yearly impact analysis and testing.

cards.title: The deadline and the skipped test
cards.situation: A digital onboarding app must launch next week. The IT head asks the Information Security Group to sign off without the planned penetration test, promising to run it after launch. You draft the reply for Maryam.

choices.text: Escalate through the CISO to the governing body and risk committee, setting out the risk and options such as delaying launch or limiting scope.
choices.outcome: Best. The independence rule exists for this moment. The decision is made by people with authority over risk, with the facts in front of them, and the bank stays inside its risk appetite.

choices.text: Agree, but ask IT to email a promise that the test will happen within a month.
choices.outcome: Partly helpful, because it creates a record, but the security function has accepted a risk it has no authority to accept and the board's risk appetite is bypassed.

choices.text: Sign off quietly; the app is small and IT owns the project.
choices.outcome: Poor. A skipped test on an internet-facing app is exactly the gap the board must know about. Security is not a rubber stamp for IT.

cards.title: Dafna Bank's yearly technology risk cycle
cards.caption: The QCB can also audit the bank's compliance at any time.

items.label: Review policies
items.detail: Cyber security policies, standards and procedures updated at least once a year

items.label: Refresh awareness
items.detail: Training content reviewed and updated at least yearly for new threats and rules

items.label: Audit
items.detail: Information systems audit covering infrastructure, people and processes at least yearly

items.label: Report to QCB
items.detail: Yearly compliance report against the regulation, signed by the board or its committee

items.label: Fix the gaps
items.detail: Material gaps remediated under board guidance; action plans shared with the QCB

cards.title: What the QCB saw in 2022
cards.caption: Source: QCB Financial Stability Review 2022. Figures are described, not quoted.

items.label: Ransomware and phishing
items.detail: Named in the QCB Financial Stability Review 2022 as cyber challenges facing the financial sector

items.label: Applications
items.detail: Security events reported by the sector concentrated on the application layer of bank environments

items.label: High
items.detail: Banks surveyed rated risk from the cyber world as very high or high

cards.title: Real case: what the QCB's 2022 review reported
cards.body:
In its **Financial Stability Review 2022**, the Qatar Central Bank described the cyber challenges of that year as **ransomware, phishing and other sophisticated attacks** that needed strong detection and response.

The review explained that the financial sector reports **key risk indicators** on security events to the QCB, and that in 2022 these events concentrated on the **application layer** of bank systems. In the QCB's survey of banks, institutions rated **risk from the cyber world** as very high or high, and also counted fraud among their high operational risks.

**Why it matters to you:** phishing is a people problem as much as a technology one. The regulator expects banks to measure awareness (learning scores, training coverage) because the same threats it sees across the sector arrive in your inbox.

cards.question: Under the QCB Technology Risks Regulation, how often must the board at least monitor the bank's cyber security indicators?
options: At least every six months
At least once every two years
Only after a critical incident
At least once every quarter, by law
cards.explanation: The regulation asks the board to monitor cyber security key indicators periodically, at least semi-annually, with senior management putting remedial plans in place. A yearly control adequacy review by senior management is a separate duty.

cards.title: Exceptions are a board decision
cards.body: If the bank cannot meet a mandatory requirement, it does not quietly ignore it. It writes a **business justification**, which the **board or a board-authorised committee approves**. Gaps found in the yearly compliance review need remediation under board guidance, and where advisory items are not met, an action plan goes to the QCB. **Common mistake:** a department head 'accepting' a risk by email. That is not an approved exception.

cards.title: Stage 1 take-aways
items: Three QCB texts work together: Technology Risks (2018), Data Handling and Protection, and Cloud Computing (in force 15 April 2024).
Personal data must also be processed in line with Law No. 13 of 2016.
The board approves cyber policy, strategy, budget and risk appetite and monitors indicators at least twice a year.
The Information Security Group is separate from IT and the CISO reports to an independent governing body.
Each year: policies reviewed, awareness refreshed, systems audited and a board-signed compliance report sent to the QCB.

cards.prompt: Think of one security rule in your bank that people see as an 'IT thing'. Who actually owns that risk under the QCB rules, and who should hear about it if it fails?

quiz.question: Which QCB regulation sets the duty to give staff information security awareness training at induction and at least yearly?
options: The Cloud Computing Regulation of 2024
Law No. 13 of 2016 on personal data
The AML/CFT Instructions for financial institutions
The Technology Risks Regulation for banks
quiz.explanation: Section 2.2 of the Technology Risks Regulation (staff competency and training) sets the awareness programme, induction training and the yearly refresher. The cloud regulation and the AML/CFT Instructions cover other topics.

quiz.question: From which date did the QCB Cloud Computing Regulation enter into force?
options: 1 January 2025
15 April 2022
15 April 2024
1 January 2018
quiz.explanation: The regulation states that it enters into force on 15 April 2024. January 2018 is the date of the Technology Risks Regulation.

quiz.question: Dafna Bank's IT head proposes that the CISO report to him because 'security is part of IT'. What does the Technology Risks Regulation expect?
options: The CISO may report to the CIO in banks with small IT teams
The CISO reports to the head of HR to keep IT and security balanced
The CISO reports to the IT head as long as the board is told about each security decision he makes
The CISO reports to an independent body and has no direct reporting line to the IT head
quiz.explanation: The regulation requires a separate Information Security Group and a CISO who reports to an independent governing body without a direct relationship to the IT head, CIO or CTO, while still working closely with them.

quiz.question: Which of these must the board of a QCB-licensed bank approve under the Technology Risks Regulation?
options: Every user's access rights
The wording of each phishing simulation email
Each individual firewall rule change
The overall cyber risk appetite
quiz.explanation: The board must approve the cyber risk appetite, policy, strategy and budget. Operational items such as firewall rules and access rights are managed by management under the approved framework.

quiz.question: A new board member asks what 'awareness and culture' indicators the board will see. Which pair fits the regulation's examples?
options: Number of servers and licence costs
Learning scores and training coverage
Share price and capital adequacy ratio
Branch footfall and customer waiting times
quiz.explanation: The regulation's cyber preparedness indicators include awareness and culture, measured by things like learning scores, training coverage and awareness-related incidents.

quiz.question: Dafna Bank cannot meet one mandatory requirement of the Technology Risks Regulation this year. What is the right route?
options: A business justification approved by the board or its authorised committee
Leave it out of the compliance report until it is fixed
Ask the vendor to sign a letter taking over the bank's responsibility for the requirement
Let the CISO accept the risk by email and close the item
quiz.explanation: Exceptions to mandatory requirements need a business justification approved by the board or its authorised committee. Hiding gaps from the compliance report or shifting responsibility to a vendor is not allowed.

quiz.question: How often must the bank, at minimum, send the QCB a compliance report based on its reporting framework for the Technology Risks Regulation?
options: Once every three years
Every month
Once a year
Only when the QCB inspects the bank
quiz.explanation: The regulation asks banks to prepare a reporting framework and submit a compliance report to the QCB at least annually, signed by the board or its authorised committee.

quiz.question: An information systems audit has just finished at Dafna Bank. Under the Technology Risks Regulation, when must the next one take place at the latest?
options: Within three years, unless the QCB asks earlier
Only when the bank replaces its core banking system
Within a year, or sooner if a change could affect security
Whenever the external auditor has spare capacity
quiz.explanation: The regulation requires an audit of information systems, covering infrastructure, people and processes, at least once a year or whenever a change may affect the bank's security.

quiz.question: Priya says the QCB Data Handling and Protection Regulation only matters to the IT department. Why is she wrong?
options: It applies only when a breach has already happened
It covers all data the institution manages and requires staff training
It applies only to paper records kept in branches and archived files held offsite
It covers only data held by outsourced vendors
quiz.explanation: The regulation applies to all financial institutions supervised by the QCB and to all data they manage, and it requires training and awareness for employees on privacy, classification and handling.

quiz.question: Under the Technology Risks Regulation, how often must cyber security policies, standards and procedures be reviewed and updated at minimum?
options: Every two years
Only when the QCB issues a new circular
At least once a year
Every five years
quiz.explanation: The regulation requires cyber security policies, standards and procedures to be reviewed and updated at least annually. New circulars may trigger earlier updates, but they are not the only trigger.

sessions.title: The Human Firewall: Awareness, Social Engineering, Acceptable Use and Fraud
sessions.summary: What the QCB requires of the bank's security awareness programme, how to recognise phishing, smishing and vishing, the acceptable use rules you sign up to, and the bank's fraud prevention training and customer education duties.
objectives: List the QCB requirements for the awareness programme: budget, yearly content review, induction, yearly refresher, assessment and records
Recognise social engineering through calls, SMS, email, social media and links, and report it correctly
Apply the acceptable use rules for email, the internet, software and confidential information
Explain the bank's fraud prevention training and its duty to educate customers about fraud and phishing

cards.title: The parcel that never came
cards.setting: Al Khor branch, Monday morning, on a video call with the Information Security Group.

lines.text: Here's what happened on Saturday. A teller got an SMS about a parcel waiting at customs, clicked the link and typed her work email and password.
The link led to a page that looked exactly like the bank's webmail login. Within minutes, someone tried to sign in from abroad.
Multi-factor authentication stopped them. And she called us twenty minutes later, which is why we reset everything fast.
She did two things wrong and one thing very right. The right thing was reporting quickly without fear.
How many others got the same SMS and said nothing?
That's the question for this stage. Our awareness programme must turn every person in this bank into a sensor, not a target.

cards.title: How the QCB wants awareness to work

scenes.heading: Funded, not optional
scenes.narration: The bank must set up a security awareness programme and give it a proper budget to launch, run and maintain it.

scenes.heading: Day one
scenes.narration: New employees receive information security awareness training as part of their wider induction, before habits form.

scenes.heading: Every year
scenes.narration: Everyone receives a refresher at least once a year. The content is reviewed at least yearly for new threats, system changes and new laws.

scenes.heading: Social engineering
scenes.narration: Staff are trained to recognise social engineering and never to disclose information that breaks bank policy, however convincing the caller.

scenes.heading: Prove it worked
scenes.narration: After training, the bank assesses whether it was effective, and keeps attendance records and each employee's acknowledgement that they received and understood it.

scenes.heading: Up to the board
scenes.narration: Senior management and board members also receive training sessions on cyber threats, because awareness must exist at every level.

cards.title: The awareness programme lifecycle at Dafna Bank

items.label: Fund
items.detail: Budget approved for launching, running and maintaining the programme

items.label: Update content
items.detail: Reviewed at least yearly for new trends, threats, systems and rules

items.label: Deliver
items.detail: At induction for new joiners; refresher at least yearly for everyone, online or classroom

items.label: Assess
items.detail: Test effectiveness after training, for example with quizzes or simulations

items.label: Record
items.detail: Keep attendance and each person's acknowledgement of understanding

items.label: Report
items.detail: Completion and learning scores go to the security committee and the board

cards.question: A contractor will sit in Dafna Bank's operations floor for two years with full system access. What does the QCB rule expect?
options: Give the contractor the same security training and access to policies as staff in that role
Skip training because contractors are trained by their own firm
Give training only if the contractor asks for it
Train the contractor only after the first incident
cards.explanation: Long-term contractors and third parties acting like staff must receive appropriate training for their role, and security material and policies must be available to relevant long-term onsite vendors and contractors.

cards.title: What the training must cover
cards.body:
The regulation lists what the awareness material must include. At Dafna Bank that means:

- the bank's **security requirements** and the **legal and regulatory** rules behind them
- **business-specific processes and controls** for your job
- the **enforcement and disciplinary process** for breaches
- **who to contact to report a security incident**
- **acceptable use** of systems, internet and email

The regulation also suggests focusing on attacks that **individual action can block**, refreshing content yearly with the **latest attack techniques**, making the refresher **mandatory for all** and **monitoring completion**. Before you even start, HR has you sign terms and a **confidentiality and non-disclosure agreement**, and you only get the access your job needs (**least privilege**).

cards.title: Social engineering or normal business?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation: is it a likely social engineering attempt, or normal business you can handle under procedure?

items.text: A caller claiming to be from QCB asks for a customer's OTP to 'verify' an account
An SMS says your parcel is held and asks you to pay a small fee by link
A gaming platform friend you have never met sends a link to 'free credits'
An email from the CEO's private webmail asks you to buy gift cards urgently
A customer at the counter shows ID and asks for her own balance
The security team announces a simulation exercise on the intranet
Your manager asks you in person to update a procedure document
A vendor's email asks you to update their bank details today, with a new account abroad

cards.title: Acceptable use: do and don't
cards.caption: The bank must teach acceptable use and basic security hygiene in its awareness courses.

items.label: Email
items.left: Use only bank email for bank work and classify messages
items.right: Send bank emails from public webmail services

items.label: Software
items.left: Use approved software installed by IT
items.right: Install or run programs of unknown origin

items.label: Suspicious mail
items.left: Report spam and attachments from strangers to security
items.right: Open attachments from strangers to check them

items.label: Sessions
items.left: Log off when you finish a task
items.right: Leave online sessions open at an empty desk

items.label: Personal data
items.left: Share only through approved channels after checks
items.right: Give personal or financial details to untrusted sources

cards.title: A call to the contact centre
cards.setting: Contact centre, Dafna Bank, Tuesday afternoon.

lines.text: A caller says he is from 'the central bank inspection team'. He knows the agent's name and the branch code.
He says a customer's account is under urgent review and asks the agent to read out the one-time password just sent to the customer's phone.
Every detail he has could come from social media or an earlier leak. The urgency is the tell.
And remember the QCB's own public advice: never share an OTP, and if a call seems fake, contact the organisation it claims to be from through official channels. No regulator needs a customer's OTP.

cards.title: The 'QCB inspector' on line 3
cards.situation: You are the contact centre agent. The caller is polite, knows internal names and says the customer could lose money if you delay. He asks for the OTP within two minutes.

choices.text: Refuse to share anything, end the call politely, note the number and report it to the security team and your supervisor straight away.
choices.outcome: Best. You protect the customer, give the security team the details to warn others and follow the training on social engineering. The real QCB never asks for OTPs.

choices.text: Ask him for his staff number and call back on the number he gives you.
choices.outcome: Partly right: you slowed down. But calling back on a number the caller supplies verifies nothing. Use only official numbers you find yourself, and report the attempt.

choices.text: Read out the OTP because he knew your name and the branch code.
choices.outcome: Poor. Knowing internal details is not proof of identity. Disclosing the OTP lets the fraudster take over the customer's account.

cards.title: Real case: the QCB's 'Stay Aware' campaign
cards.body:
Qatar Central Bank launched a national information security awareness campaign called **'Stay Aware'**, together with the **Ministry of Interior**, the **National Cyber Security Agency** and the **QFC Regulatory Authority**.

The campaign names the main channels for cyber fraud as **phone calls, social media, emails, SMS messages and links**. Its tips tell the public not to reveal personal information by phone, never to share card details or **one-time passwords**, to avoid opening links in SMS messages, to be wary of messages demanding urgent action and to contact the impersonated organisation through its official channels.

It also gives reporting routes for financial cybercrime, including a Ministry of Interior hotline and the Metrash2 app.

**Why it matters to you:** customers will repeat these messages back to you. Your behaviour on the phone must match what the regulator tells them.

cards.title: Lures and how to spot them

cards.back: Lures you to open a link or attachment or reveal information. Check the sender address, distrust urgency, report it.
Phishing by SMS, often posing as banks, couriers or popular websites. Do not open the link; contact the sender officially.
Phishing by voice call. Callers sound official and rushed. Never disclose OTPs, passwords or card details.
A web address one letter away from the bank's. The bank must monitor new registrations of similar domains.
Messages from unknown accounts or fake friends with links, often to take over accounts or blackmail.
A made-up story, such as an audit or an urgent transfer, built to make you skip a control.

cards.title: Reporting a suspicious email at Dafna Bank
cards.prompt: Put the steps in the right order.
steps: Notice the warning signs: unknown sender, urgency, odd link
Do not click links or open attachments
Report it to the security team using the bank's reporting channel
Delete it once the security team has what it needs
Tell the team at once if you already clicked or typed a password

cards.title: Fraud training and customer education
cards.body:
Section 10 of the Technology Risks Regulation adds fraud duties that touch every front-line role:

- The bank must run **training on fraud prevention practices** in various forums, delivered by the **fraud management team**. The fraud risk team itself must keep training continuously.
- The bank must give **customers continuous fraud risk awareness**, educate them on **cyber security risks** and the danger of **sharing login credentials**, and encourage them to **report phishing emails and sites**, then act on those reports.
- For email, the bank should give customers an address to forward suspicious messages, harden its own email and domain settings, and **inform the QCB of every phishing incident** it discovers.
- Frauds in **merchant acquiring** must be reported to the QCB, and the bank must share data the police request when fraudulent money lands in its accounts, even if the bank is not the victim.

cards.question: Which team does the QCB Technology Risks Regulation say should deliver fraud prevention training to employees?
options: The fraud management team
The external auditor
The marketing team
The board's audit committee
cards.explanation: The regulation says training on fraud prevention practices must be conducted at various forums and undertaken by the fraud management team, which itself must train continuously.

cards.title: Stage 2 take-aways
items: Awareness training happens at induction and at least yearly, with content reviewed every year.
Training must teach staff to recognise social engineering and never disclose information against policy.
The bank assesses effectiveness and keeps attendance and acknowledgement records.
Never share OTPs or passwords; report suspicious calls, SMS and emails at once, even if you clicked.
Fraud prevention training comes from the fraud team; customers must be educated and every phishing incident is reported to the QCB.

cards.prompt: Which lure would most likely work on you: a rushed call, a parcel SMS or an email from a senior manager? What will you do differently next time one arrives?

quiz.question: A new teller joins Dafna Bank on Sunday. Under the QCB Technology Risks Regulation, when should she receive information security awareness training?
options: As part of her wider induction programme
Only when the next yearly refresher opens
Only once she has worked for a full year
Only if she later handles customer data
quiz.explanation: The regulation requires information security awareness training for new employees as part of the wider induction programme, followed by a refresher at least yearly.

quiz.question: What is the minimum frequency for the security awareness refresher for existing staff?
options: Every quarter for all staff
Only after a reported incident
At least once every two years
At least once a year
quiz.explanation: Refresher training must be conducted at least annually. Some banks run it more often, but yearly is the floor set by the regulation.

quiz.question: Dafna Bank's HR team wants to drop the post-training quiz to save time. Which QCB expectation would that break?
options: Assessing training effectiveness after the training
Translating training into every customer's language before staff take it
Sending training records to the police
Holding training only in a classroom
quiz.explanation: The regulation asks banks to perform an assessment after training to check its effectiveness, and to keep attendance records and acknowledgements. Classroom delivery is optional; online training is allowed.

quiz.question: Which record must Dafna Bank keep for each employee after security awareness training, according to the regulation?
options: A list of every website the employee visited during and after the training session
Attendance and the employee's acknowledgement of understanding
A copy of the employee's personal social media profile
The employee's home internet provider and router type
quiz.explanation: Attendance records and each employee's acknowledgement of having received and understood the training should be kept. Collecting unrelated personal data would breach data minimisation.

quiz.question: A caller says he is from Qatar Central Bank and asks an agent for a customer's one-time password to stop a fraud. What should the agent do?
options: Give the OTP because regulators can request any data
Give only the first three digits as a test
Refuse, end the call and report it to the security team
Transfer the call to the customer so he can ask directly
quiz.explanation: No legitimate authority needs a customer's OTP. Training must teach staff to recognise social engineering and not disclose information against policy. Reporting lets the bank warn others.

quiz.question: Which item does the regulation say must be part of the security training material?
options: Each department's annual budget
Passwords for shared test accounts
Contact details for reporting security incidents
The CISO's personal mobile number only
quiz.explanation: The training material must include the bank's security requirements, legal and regulatory requirements, processes and controls, the disciplinary process, contacts for reporting incidents and acceptable use.

quiz.question: A relationship manager wants to send a large client file from her personal webmail because the bank's mail server is slow. What do the acceptable use rules say?
options: It is allowed if the client agrees by phone
It is allowed after working hours only
Public webmail must not be used to send email from bank systems
It is allowed if the file is zipped and password protected before it is sent
quiz.explanation: The regulation states that public webmail services shall not be used to send emails from the bank's systems. Data must move through approved, secure channels.

quiz.question: Dafna Bank discovers a phishing website copying its online banking login page. Besides acting to take it down, what does the regulation require?
options: Post the fake site's address on social media for customers
Inform the QCB about the phishing incident
Inform only the hosting company that runs the site
Wait to see whether any customer complains first
quiz.explanation: The anti-phishing section requires the bank to inform the QCB about the discovery of all phishing incidents and to preserve evidence for possible prosecution.

quiz.question: Which statement about customer fraud awareness matches the Technology Risks Regulation?
options: Customer education is the QCB's job, not the bank's
Customer awareness is optional for retail banks
The bank must keep educating customers and encourage them to report phishing
Banks may educate customers only once at account opening
quiz.explanation: The bank must provide continuous fraud risk awareness, improve customer cyber awareness, encourage reporting of phishing emails and sites and act on those reports.

quiz.question: A supplier's long-term on-site engineer asks why he must sign a confidentiality agreement. What does the regulation require?
options: Staff, contractors and third parties sign terms and an NDA on joining
A verbal promise is enough for staff working fewer than two years
Agreements are needed only for staff in the IT department
Only permanent staff sign; contractors are covered by their own employer's agreements
quiz.explanation: The regulation asks banks to ensure that employees, contractors and third-party staff sign terms and conditions and a confidentiality and non-disclosure agreement when joining or changing role.

sessions.title: Handling Customer Data: The QCB Data Handling and Protection Regulation
sessions.summary: How the QCB data regulation organises data governance and the Data Privacy Officer, how PII, sensitive personal and sensitive financial information are classified and processed, where data must live, how long it is kept, and what customers can ask for.
objectives: Describe the data governance unit and the Data Privacy Officer's role, independence and reporting line
Classify PII, sensitive personal information, sensitive financial information and technical information
Apply the three bases for processing, consent rules and customer rights
State the QCB rules on data location, third parties, impact assessments and minimum retention periods

cards.title: The marketing spreadsheet
cards.setting: Priya's office, Data Privacy Office, Dafna Bank head office.

lines.text: Marketing wants to send our premium customer list, with salaries and card limits, to an events agency for a gala invitation.
Is the agency a third party processing our data? Do we have consent for marketing use?
That's my point. Salaries and card limits are sensitive financial information. They sit in our highest classification tier.
And where would the agency store it? Their cloud drive might be anywhere in the world.
Welcome to the Pearl Vault. In this stage you learn to treat customer data like the pearls this coast was famous for: counted, classified and never handed over casually.

cards.title: Who looks after data at Dafna Bank

scenes.heading: A data governance unit
scenes.narration: Every QCB-regulated institution must set up a data governance unit or give the job to an existing function. It builds the privacy programme and works with security, risk, IT and compliance.

scenes.heading: A Data Privacy Officer
scenes.narration: The bank must appoint a Data Privacy Officer with real privacy knowledge, notify the QCB and submit the fit and proper form under the QCB licensing rules.

scenes.heading: Independent and senior
scenes.narration: The DPO must be free of conflicts, must not be involved in the bank's operations and reports directly to the chief executive, who makes sure privacy risks reach the board.

scenes.heading: Everyone keeps learning
scenes.narration: The bank must give employees and relevant stakeholders training and awareness so they keep their knowledge of privacy, classification, handling, stewardship, backup and recovery up to date.

cards.title: Data classes under the QCB regulation
cards.caption: SFI includes card information, account information, transactions, loans and credit scores.

items.label: SPI and SFI
items.detail: Sensitive personal and sensitive financial information: always the highest, strictest classification tier

items.label: PII
items.detail: Personal data that can identify a person, such as names, ID numbers and contact details; classified by the bank's framework

items.label: Technical information
items.detail: Confidential system data such as user credentials and network, system, application and security logs

items.label: Other data
items.detail: Classified under the bank's own policy and handling guideline

cards.title: Which class of data?
cards.prompt: Sort each item into the class the QCB data regulation would give it.

items.text: A customer's credit score
Card numbers and card limits
A customer's account transaction history
A customer's name and mobile number
A customer's Qatar ID number on a form
Firewall and application logs
Service account passwords
Health details given for a loan insurance claim

cards.question: Under the QCB data regulation, how must sensitive financial information be classified?
options: Under the highest, strictest classification tier the bank has
Under the lowest tier, because banks hold so much of it
Under any tier the business owner prefers
It does not need to be classified at all
cards.explanation: The regulation defines sensitive financial information, such as card and account data, transactions, loans and credit scores, and requires it to be managed under the most strict classification available. The same applies to sensitive personal information.

cards.title: When may the bank process personal data?
cards.body:
The regulation allows the bank to process PII, SPI and SFI only when at least one of three bases applies:

1. the customer has given **explicit consent**
2. the processing is needed for a **regulatory or legal** activity
3. the processing is needed to **fulfil a contract**

Consent is expected, for example, before **sharing data with a third party**, using data for **marketing**, or using **sensitive personal information**, unless a legal, regulatory or contractual basis applies. Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, and customers can **refuse or withdraw** it at any time except where the law or a contract requires the processing. The bank must tell customers what happens if they do not consent, and keep a **record of each consent**: purpose, who gave it, date, method and the privacy policy then in force.

Collect only what you need to serve the customer or meet legal duties.

cards.title: Customer requests and what the bank must offer
cards.prompt: Match each customer request to what the regulation says the bank must do.

pairs.right: Confirm whether their personal data is being processed
Provide a copy in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format
Delete it where this does not break retention, contract or legal duties
Restrict processing of incorrect or inaccurate data

pairs.left: A parent opens an account for a child
pairs.right: Check the person consenting holds parental responsibility

cards.title: Where does the data live?
cards.setting: Data governance committee, the next morning.

lines.text: The new analytics platform is cheaper if the main database sits in a data centre abroad.
For PII, SPI and SFI, the primary storage and processing environment must be inside Qatar. Abroad only with explicit QCB approval.
And any foreign storage or transfer of personal data needs QCB approval plus due diligence on the jurisdiction and the third party.
So the cheap option comes with a regulator's approval process. Let's price that in.

cards.title: The gala invitation list
cards.situation: Marketing insists the events agency needs the premium customer list with names, mobile numbers, salaries and card limits by tomorrow. Customers have not consented to marketing use or third-party sharing.

choices.text: Refuse the full file; check consent, send only the minimum fields to consenting customers after the agency's data protection checks and contract are in place, and involve the DPO.
choices.outcome: Best. Marketing and third-party sharing need consent, sensitive financial data has no place in an invitation list, and the agency must be assessed and bound by contract before receiving anything.

choices.text: Send names and mobile numbers only, without checking consent, because they are not sensitive.
choices.outcome: Partly better, since salaries and limits are removed, but PII still needs a lawful basis and consent for marketing and third-party sharing.

choices.text: Send the full file because the gala is good for customer relationships.
choices.outcome: Poor. It shares SFI with an unassessed third party without consent and breaches the bank's classification rules and bank secrecy expectations.

cards.title: Minimum retention periods in the QCB data regulation
cards.caption: These are minimums. Keep data longer where another law or regulation requires it, including AML/CFT rules.

items.label: Sensitive financial information
items.detail: Card, account, transaction, loan and credit score data

items.label: Personal data, PII and SPI
items.detail: Customer and employee personal data of all kinds

items.label: Technical information
items.detail: Credentials and system, network, application and security logs

items.label: All other data
items.detail: Set by the bank's own retention policy

cards.back: Record of Processing Activities: what data, from where, why, on what basis, how long, who sees it. Reviewed yearly or on major change.
A picture of how data flows through processes and systems. Data maps are reviewed yearly or on major change.
Required for new sensitive processes, changes to them, and significant changes to relevant laws.
Guidance for staff on handling data, published so the people who need it can find and use it.
Public statement telling customers their rights and how data is collected, used, shared and kept.
The QCB must approve processing within fully autonomous decision-making systems before it starts.

cards.title: Example: a vendor's quiet breach
cards.body:
Dafna Bank uses a printing company to send card PIN mailers. One Thursday the printer's IT manager realises a laptop with a batch file of customer names and addresses was stolen from a car.

Because the bank's contract followed the QCB regulation, the printer had to **report breaches involving the bank's data promptly to a designated representative** at the bank. Priya was told within hours, not weeks.

The contract also included **data protection, confidentiality and compliance clauses**, the bank had **assessed the printer's controls** before signing, and the printer only received the fields it needed. That is the regulation's approach to third parties: assess first, contract clearly, share the minimum and require prompt breach reports.

Stage 4 will follow what happens next: the breach becomes an incident, with reports to the authorities.

cards.question: A customer asks Dafna Bank to delete all her data after closing her account. What should the bank do?
options: Delete what it can, keeping data that retention or legal duties still require
Delete everything at once, including transaction records
Refuse, because closed accounts have no rights
Keep everything forever in case of future disputes
cards.explanation: Customers can request deletion, but the bank's deletion policy must not break retention, contract or legal requirements. Transaction and personal data have 10-year minimum retention periods under the regulation.

cards.title: Bank secrecy still applies
cards.body: The data regulation reminds institutions to respect **bank secrecy** under the QCB Law, especially for sensitive financial information. Even inside the bank, look up customer data only when your job needs it. **Common mistake:** 'just checking' a famous customer's balance out of curiosity. Using data beyond your legitimate permissions is a **data privacy breach**, even though you are an authorised user.

cards.title: Stage 3 take-aways
items: Every QCB-regulated institution needs a data governance unit and an independent DPO reporting to the CEO.
SPI and SFI always sit in the highest classification tier.
Process personal data only with explicit consent, a legal or regulatory need, or to fulfil a contract.
The primary environment for PII, SPI and SFI is in Qatar; foreign storage or transfer needs QCB approval.
Minimum retention: 10 years for SFI and personal data, 1 year for technical information.

cards.prompt: Pick one spreadsheet or report you handle that contains customer data. Which class is it, who else receives it, and is there a lawful basis for each recipient?

quiz.question: Which person must every QCB-regulated financial institution appoint under the Data Handling and Protection Regulation?
options: An external data broker
A Data Sales Manager
A Data Privacy Officer
A Chief Marketing Officer
quiz.explanation: The regulation requires a Data Privacy Officer with the necessary knowledge and experience, notification to the QCB and the fit and proper form under the licensing rules.

quiz.question: Dafna Bank plans to make the head of retail operations its DPO as an extra hat. What is the problem under the regulation?
options: The DPO must always be a lawyer by training
The DPO must report to the head of IT
The DPO must not be involved in the institution's operations
The DPO must be employed by an outside firm
quiz.explanation: The DPO can be an existing role only if independent and free of conflicts, and must not be involved in operations. The DPO reports directly to the CEO or most senior manager.

quiz.question: Which item is sensitive financial information under the QCB data regulation?
options: A customer's credit score
A customer's preferred language for letters
The bank's public exchange rate table
The bank's published branch opening hours
quiz.explanation: Sensitive financial information covers data such as card information, account information, transactions, loans and credit scores linked to a customer.

quiz.question: Which is NOT one of the three bases on which the regulation lets a bank process PII, SPI and SFI?
options: Processing is needed for a regulatory or legal activity
The data would be commercially useful to a partner
The customer has given explicit consent
Processing is required to fulfil a contract
quiz.explanation: The regulation lists explicit consent, regulatory or legal necessity and contract fulfilment. Commercial usefulness to someone else is not a lawful basis.

quiz.question: Dafna Bank wants to run its main customer database for PII and SFI in a data centre abroad. What does the regulation require?
options: The customer's verbal agreement during the next branch visit
Only a notification to the NCSA after the migration is complete and the data has moved abroad
Explicit approval from the QCB before using a primary environment outside Qatar
Nothing, if the data centre is certified to an international standard
quiz.explanation: The primary storage and processing environment for PII, SPI and SFI must be in Qatar; using one abroad needs explicit QCB approval, and foreign storage or transfer generally needs QCB approval and due diligence.

quiz.question: What is the minimum retention period for technical information such as system and security logs under the data regulation?
options: Ten years
Three months
Five years
One year
quiz.explanation: The retention table sets 10 years for SFI and for personal data, PII and SPI, and 1 year for technical information, unless another law requires longer.

quiz.question: A customer withdraws marketing consent but still has an active personal loan. What follows?
options: The loan must be closed because all consent, for every purpose, is now withdrawn
The bank may keep marketing if it reduces the frequency
Marketing stops; processing needed for the loan contract continues
Nothing changes until the loan matures
quiz.explanation: Customers can refuse or withdraw consent at any time, except where processing is needed for legal or regulatory obligations or to fulfil a contract. Marketing depends on consent; servicing the loan does not.

quiz.question: Which record must the bank keep when a customer gives consent?
options: Only the customer's signature, with no date
The customer's social media handles and contacts
A recording of every phone call ever made by the customer
Purpose, who consented, the date and method, and the privacy policy in force
quiz.explanation: The regulation lists the purpose, the identity of the person consenting, the date, the method, the External Privacy Policy then in force and related documents.

quiz.question: When must the bank carry out a Privacy Impact Assessment under the regulation?
options: Only once, when the bank receives its licence and before it opens its first branch
For new or changed sensitive processes, or major changes in relevant laws
Only after a customer complaint
Only when the external auditor asks for one
quiz.explanation: A PIA is needed for new activities involving sensitive processes, changes to sensitive processes and significant changes in relevant laws that may affect privacy.

quiz.question: An authorised employee browses a celebrity customer's transactions out of curiosity. How does the regulation describe this?
options: Not a breach, because the employee had system access
A data privacy breach, because an authorised user exceeded legitimate permissions
A data breach only if the data leaves the bank's systems and reaches an outside party
A matter for HR only, with no data protection angle
quiz.explanation: The regulation defines a data privacy breach as personal data being accessed or used by an authorised person beyond legitimate permissions or for unauthorised purposes. A data breach involves unauthorised individuals.

sessions.title: Incidents and Breaches: Escalation, the 1-Hour Report and Data Breach Duties
sessions.summary: How Dafna Bank detects, classifies and escalates security incidents, why every user must know how to report, how critical incidents reach the QCB within one hour, and how data breaches are reported to the QCB, the NCSA and the Ministry of Interior.
objectives: Describe the incident management framework: owner, central severity setting, evidence and lessons learned
Explain why every user is trained to report incidents and how to report one
Apply the rule that critical incidents go to the QCB and relevant authorities within 1 hour of identification
Handle data breaches and data privacy breaches under section 16 of the QCB data regulation

cards.title: Thursday, 4:12 pm
cards.setting: Security operations room, Dafna Bank head office.

lines.text: An alert flashes: dozens of file servers are renaming files at high speed. A branch manager calls the help desk saying her shared drive shows strange file names.
Could be ransomware. Could be a backup job gone wrong. The next hour decides a lot.
Start the clock from identification. If the central team classes this as critical, the QCB and the relevant authorities must hear from us within one hour.
Those servers hold customer files. If data was copied out, this is also a data breach.
I'll get the crisis team ready in case we need to switch to recovery sites.
And the branch manager who called the help desk instead of rebooting? She just bought us twenty minutes.

cards.title: How an incident moves through Dafna Bank

scenes.heading: Someone notices
scenes.narration: Monitoring tools raise alerts automatically, but people spot many incidents first. Every user is trained to report incidents to the incident management team.

scenes.heading: Evaluate
scenes.narration: The team checks whether it is a false alarm or hoax, and how big the problem is.

scenes.heading: Classify centrally
scenes.narration: A central incident response team sets the severity level, so resolution times and escalation match the risk.

scenes.heading: Escalate and report
scenes.narration: Critical incidents are reported to the QCB and the relevant government authorities within one hour of identification. Large incidents keep the QCB and the Ministry of Interior informed.

scenes.heading: Contain, recover, learn
scenes.narration: The team contains the incident, restores service, collects evidence that can stand up legally, finds the root cause and records lessons learned.

cards.title: Incident lifecycle under the QCB Technology Risks Regulation

items.label: Detect and report
items.detail: Tools alert automatically; users report to the incident management team

items.label: Evaluate
items.detail: False trigger or real? What type and how large?

items.label: Prioritise
items.detail: Central team sets severity and the matching escalation route

items.label: Notify
items.detail: Critical incidents to the QCB and relevant authorities within 1 hour

items.label: Contain and recover
items.detail: Find the source, contain, assess damage, restore and monitor

items.label: Learn
items.detail: Root cause analysis, documentation and lessons learned

cards.question: Under the QCB Technology Risks Regulation, how quickly must a critical incident be reported to the QCB and the relevant government authorities?
options: Within 1 hour of identification
Within 72 hours of identification
Within 24 hours of the root cause being known
By the end of the next business day
cards.explanation: Item 8.2.10 requires all critical incidents to be reported to the QCB and the relevant governmental authorities within 1 hour of identification. Waiting for a root cause would miss the deadline.

cards.title: Who does what in incident management
cards.body:
The regulation expects a clear structure rather than heroics:

- **An owner.** One person owns and manages the incident management programme, its budget and its execution, and is the contact point for security communications.
- **Dedicated resources** with documented roles for recording, analysing, fixing and monitoring incidents.
- **Central severity setting** by an incident response team, so a branch and a data centre are judged by the same scale.
- **A communication plan** for reporting internally and externally, to the QCB and agencies such as the Ministry of Interior, with public relations involved.
- **Evidence** collected and kept so it meets the rules of evidence if legal action follows.
- **Yearly testing** of the escalation and response plan against scenarios such as ransomware, extortion and denial of service.
- **Specialised training** for people who handle incidents, and post-incident reviews.

cards.title: Report it now or handle it normally?
cards.prompt: As an ordinary employee, which of these should you report to the incident management team straight away?

items.text: You typed your password into a page that turned out to be fake
Your laptop with customer files was stolen from your car
Files on a shared drive are suddenly renamed with odd extensions
A USB stick you do not recognise is plugged into a branch PC
You sent a customer statement to the wrong customer by email
You need a new printer cartridge
You forgot your password and need a routine reset
You want a second monitor for your desk

lines.text: Update: the malware encrypted files on three servers. Logs show about 2 GB went to an unknown address before we cut the link.
Then we treat it as a data breach too. The QCB data regulation says every data breach is classified as an incident and follows QCB incident reporting.
So the QCB hears from us, and the data rule adds the National Cyber Security Agency and the Ministry of Interior.
We also assess the impact now, decide whether customers must be told, and prompt staff and customers to act, for example to watch for fraud.
(by phone) I need a one-page summary for the board tonight. What do we know, and what have we told the regulator?

cards.title: Security incident duties and data breach duties
cards.caption: One event can trigger both sets of duties. Run them together, not one after the other.

items.label: Main source
items.right: Data Handling and Protection Regulation, section 16

items.label: Who is told
items.left: The QCB and relevant government authorities; QCB and MOI kept informed of large incidents
items.right: The QCB and authorised agencies including the NCSA and the Ministry of Interior

items.label: Timing
items.left: Critical incidents within 1 hour of identification
items.right: As set by QCB incident reporting guidelines, since a breach is an incident

items.label: Extra steps
items.left: Root cause, evidence, lessons learned, yearly plan test
items.right: Assess impact, decide on telling customers, trigger action to limit harm

cards.title: The 4:55 pm decision
cards.situation: The central incident team has rated the event critical at 4:20 pm. Legal suggests waiting until tomorrow to report to the QCB, 'when we have the full picture'. It is now 4:55 pm.

choices.text: Report to the QCB and relevant authorities now with what is known, state what is still unknown, and send updates as the picture develops.
choices.outcome: Best. The 1-hour clock runs from identification, not from full understanding. An early, honest report with follow-ups meets the rule and builds trust.

choices.text: Send a short email to a QCB contact saying 'possible issue, details tomorrow'.
choices.outcome: Partly right on timing, but a vague note without the incident's nature, impact and actions may not meet the bank's reporting procedure or the QCB's expectations.

choices.text: Wait until tomorrow so the report is complete and accurate.
choices.outcome: Poor. The deadline would be missed by many hours. Completeness comes through updates, not by delaying the first report.

cards.back: An incident in the highest severity class. Report to the QCB and relevant authorities within 1 hour of identification.
Sensitive, confidential or protected data accessed, disclosed or stolen by unauthorised people.
Personal data used by an authorised person beyond their permissions or for improper purposes.
For major incidents: timeline, losses, costs, customers affected, reputational impact and corrective actions.
Evidence collected and kept so it meets legal rules if the bank pursues action.
Documented findings from each incident, used to improve how future incidents are handled.

cards.title: Your first moves if you think you caused an incident
cards.prompt: You clicked a link and typed your password. Put your actions in the right order.
steps: Stop: do not type anything else or open more links
Report it at once to the incident management team through the bank's channel
Follow their instructions, such as disconnecting or changing passwords
Write down what you saw and when, for the investigation
Join the follow-up review and share what made the lure convincing

cards.question: Under section 16 of the QCB data regulation, which authorities must be told of a data breach besides the QCB?
options: The National Cyber Security Agency and the Ministry of Interior
The Ministry of Commerce and the stock exchange
Only the bank's external auditor
No one else; the QCB passes it on
cards.explanation: The regulation requires data breaches and data privacy breaches to be reported to the QCB and the authorised agencies in Qatar, including the NCSA and the Ministry of Interior.

cards.title: Example: a shared ATM network fraud
cards.body:
Over a weekend, criminals use cloned cards issued by another bank to withdraw cash at Dafna Bank ATMs on a shared network.

Under the Technology Risks Regulation, in a shared ATM network the **acquiring bank reports the fraud**, not the card issuer. Dafna Bank, as acquirer, reports it and asks the issuing bank for help recovering the money.

The incident team keeps the ATM logs and camera footage as **evidence**, the fraud team checks whether Dafna's own customers were affected, and the bank shares the data the police request. If the fraud had happened in the bank's **merchant acquiring** business, it would have to be reported to the QCB.

**Lesson:** fraud and cyber incidents overlap. Know which team leads and which reports go where.

cards.title: Reporting without fear
cards.body: The fastest incident reports come from people who are not afraid of blame. Dafna Bank's policy separates **honest mistakes reported quickly** from **deliberate breaches**, which follow the disciplinary process. **Common mistake:** trying to fix it yourself first, for example rebooting an infected PC, which can destroy evidence and waste minutes of the 1-hour window.

cards.title: Stage 4 take-aways
items: Every user is trained to report incidents to the incident management team.
A central team sets severity; critical incidents go to the QCB and relevant authorities within 1 hour of identification.
Report early with what you know and update later; never wait for the full picture.
A data breach is an incident: report to the QCB, the NCSA and the Ministry of Interior, assess impact and decide on telling customers.
Keep evidence, find the root cause, record lessons learned and test the response plan every year.

cards.prompt: Do you know, without searching, how to reach your bank's incident team right now? If not, find out today and save the contact where you will see it.

quiz.question: Who sets the severity level of an incident at Dafna Bank under the QCB Technology Risks Regulation?
options: The employee who first noticed it
The branch manager where it happened
The vendor whose system was affected
A centralised incident response team
quiz.explanation: The regulation asks banks to delegate the job of determining and assigning incident severity levels to a centralised incident response team, so severity is judged consistently.

quiz.question: Why does the regulation integrate incident management with security awareness training?
options: So every user knows how to report incidents to the incident team
So incident reports can be skipped for trained staff
So staff learn how to remove malware from their own PCs without bothering the incident team
So the training team can investigate incidents itself
quiz.explanation: Item 8.2.9 says the incident process is integrated with awareness training, all users are trained to report incidents and to respond to certain events such as fire.

quiz.question: A critical incident is identified at 10:05 am. By when, at the latest, should the QCB and the relevant authorities have the report?
options: Once the root cause analysis is approved
11:05 am the same day
The end of the same week
10:05 am the next day
quiz.explanation: Critical incidents must be reported within 1 hour of identification, so 11:05 am. Root cause analysis comes later and does not delay the report.

quiz.question: Which scenarios does the regulation say the yearly test of the incident escalation and response plan should simulate?
options: Only fire evacuation of the head office
Only a change in the bank's share price
Only failures of the staff canteen systems
Attacks such as ransomware, extortion and denial of service
quiz.explanation: The predetermined escalation and response plan must be tested every year to simulate responses to attacks such as ransomware, extortion, DDoS and level 1 severity incidents.

quiz.question: During an incident, an engineer wants to wipe and rebuild an infected server immediately to save time. What concern does the regulation raise?
options: Rebuilding servers is banned during business hours
Evidence must be kept so it meets legal rules of evidence
Servers can only be rebuilt by the QCB
The vendor must approve every rebuild in writing first, even during a live incident
quiz.explanation: Evidence related to incidents must be collected, retained and presented in line with the rules of evidence where legal action may follow. Wiping first can destroy it.

quiz.question: Customer data was copied out during a cyber attack. Under the QCB data regulation, how should Dafna Bank treat the data breach?
options: As a routine IT ticket closed within a month
As an incident, following QCB incident reporting guidelines
As a private matter between the bank and its insurer
As a marketing issue for the communications team
quiz.explanation: Section 16 requires any data breach or data privacy breach to be classified as an incident and reported under QCB incident reporting guidelines, to the QCB, NCSA and Ministry of Interior.

quiz.question: After a data breach, what must the bank assess about its customers under section 16?
options: Whether they should be asked to sign a waiver
Whether they can be charged for the investigation
Whether their accounts should be closed
Whether the breach needs to be reported to them
quiz.explanation: The regulation requires the bank to assess the impact of the breach on identification and to assess the need to report it to customers, then trigger action to limit harm.

quiz.question: In a shared ATM network, cloned cards from Bank B are used at Bank A's ATMs. Who reports the fraud under the regulation?
options: Bank A, as the acquirer, with help from Bank B to recover funds
Only the customer whose card was cloned
Bank B alone, because it issued the cards
Neither bank; the ATM network operator reports
quiz.explanation: In a shared ATM network, the acquirer reports the fraud and seeks the issuer's help in recovering the money.

quiz.question: A vendor processing Dafna Bank's customer data suffers a breach. What must the bank's contract and procedures ensure?
options: The vendor reports only if customers complain
The vendor handles it alone and tells the bank about it at the next contract renewal
The vendor reports only to its own regulator abroad
The vendor promptly reports it to a designated representative at the bank
quiz.explanation: The data regulation requires institutions to ensure third parties promptly report data breaches and data privacy breaches involving the institution's data to a designated representative.

quiz.question: Which document must Dafna Bank prepare so incidents are reported both internally and externally, including to the QCB and agencies such as the Ministry of Interior?
options: A communication plan and procedure for reporting security incidents
A marketing campaign plan explaining new products and services to customers and the press
A list of preferred printing suppliers
A staff holiday rota for the security team
quiz.explanation: Item 8.2.8 requires a communication plan and procedure for reporting incidents internally and externally, involving public relations or communications functions.

sessions.title: Resilience, Cloud and the Bank's Programme: Continuity, Cloud Arrangements and Assessment Readiness
sessions.summary: What the QCB expects for business continuity and cyber crisis plans, how the Cloud Computing Regulation governs cloud arrangements, and how the bank's whole programme of training, records, audit and reporting comes together for the QCB.
objectives: Describe the BCM roles, yearly testing, test types and unplanned drills required by the QCB
Explain the cyber crisis management plan and why incident handlers need specialised training
Apply the main Cloud Computing Regulation duties: accountability, register, due diligence, approval, continuity and exit
Summarise the bank's yearly programme: training records, audit, compliance reporting and board oversight

cards.title: The drill nobody announced
cards.setting: Business continuity command centre, Lusail, 7:30 am, Wednesday.

lines.text: Phones buzz across the bank: the head office is 'unavailable' and critical teams must move to the recovery site in Lusail.
Good morning. This is one of our unplanned drills. Only a handful of people knew. Let's see how ready we really are.
Payments are up at the recovery site. But the card system runs on a cloud service, and I've never tested the switch-over with the provider.
Then that's our finding for today. The cloud provider has to be part of our continuity tests.
(arriving) The board will read this drill report. Tell me what failed, not just what worked.
Welcome to the last stage. Today you see how resilience, cloud and the whole programme fit together before the QCB looks at it.

scenes.heading: A senior owner
scenes.narration: A senior manager is designated as head of business continuity. They own the plan, keep it current, make sure impact analysis, risk assessment and testing happen at least yearly, and advise management on declaring a crisis.

scenes.heading: A senior committee
scenes.narration: A committee of senior officials from areas such as IT, HR, legal, business and information security runs drills, decides when to activate the plan and owns continuity communication, training and awareness across the bank.

scenes.heading: Yearly testing
scenes.narration: Every year the bank tests its plans: table-top discussions, simulations that train people in crisis roles, technical recovery, disaster recovery, supplier tests and full rehearsals.

scenes.heading: Surprise drills
scenes.narration: At least four unplanned drills a year, with at least one hot test that moves activities to the alternate site and three cold tests of selected parts of the plan.

scenes.heading: Report and improve
scenes.narration: Internal audit reviews the testing programme, an independent external audit happens yearly, and the bank sends an approved copy of its plan with results to the QCB each year.

cards.title: Choosing the right continuity test
cards.caption: The QCB expects all of these within the yearly testing programme, plus supplier tests.

items.label: Table-top
items.detail: Discuss recovery using example interruptions; low disruption, builds shared understanding

items.label: Simulation
items.detail: Rehearse post-incident and crisis roles so people learn their parts

items.label: Technical recovery and DR
items.detail: Restore systems and run operations from the recovery site

items.label: Complete rehearsal
items.detail: Test people, equipment, facilities and processes together in a crisis

cards.question: How many unplanned business continuity drills must a bank run each year at minimum under the Technology Risks Regulation?
options: Four, with at least one hot test and three cold tests
One, announced in advance to all staff
Two, both table-top discussions
Twelve, one every month
cards.explanation: The regulation requires at least four unplanned BCM drills a year, at least one hot and three cold, with only a restricted group of people aware beforehand.

cards.title: The cyber crisis management plan
cards.body:
The regulation recognises that ordinary continuity plans may not be enough for cyber attacks. Banks must have a **Cyber Crisis Management Plan (CCMP)** covering four things: **detection, response, recovery and containment**.

The CCMP sets out incident severity and types, signs of compromise, detection methods, reporting channels, threat information sharing and the expected response for each scenario, plus controls to **quarantine** affected devices.

Two people points stand out:

- the bank must give **specialised training to personnel who handle incidents**, review incidents afterwards and test response plans periodically
- **working from home** should not be used for staff in critical functions; highly privileged users may connect remotely only with **prior approval** and when needed

Plans also need a **trained media spokesperson**, draft press releases and regular **communication drills**.

cards.title: Business continuity or cloud regulation?
cards.prompt: Sort each duty to the QCB text it comes from.

items.text: Run at least four unplanned drills a year
Send an approved copy of the BCP to the QCB yearly
Appoint a senior head of business continuity
Keep a register of all cloud arrangements
Disclose the full register to the QCB every year
Get QCB approval before signing a material cloud arrangement
Plan both a stressed exit and a managed exit
Keep a trained media spokesperson for crises

cards.title: Cloud under the QCB Cloud Computing Regulation

scenes.heading: Strategy and accountability
scenes.narration: A regulated entity needs a cloud strategy, a risk appetite for cloud and a function that oversees cloud arrangements. Outsourcing to the cloud never outsources accountability.

scenes.heading: Register
scenes.narration: The entity keeps a register of every cloud arrangement, marks which are material, discloses its materiality criteria to the QCB and gives the QCB the full register every year.

scenes.heading: Due diligence and approval
scenes.narration: Before contracting, it checks the provider, its sub-contractors and locations, runs risk and threat assessments and gets QCB approval for material arrangements.

scenes.heading: Contract
scenes.narration: Contracts give the bank and the QCB access and audit rights, require incident reports without undue delay, notice of sub-contracting and protection of personal data under Law 13 of 2016.

scenes.heading: Continuity and exit
scenes.narration: Cloud services are built into continuity plans and tests, and every arrangement has an exit plan for both a calm and a stressed exit.

cards.title: The cloud card system
cards.setting: Lusail command centre, after the drill.

lines.text: The drill showed we can't switch the card platform to the provider's recovery region on our own. We've never tested it together.
The cloud regulation is clear: integrate the provider into our business continuity tests and document how to switch over and back.
And personal and financial information must be processed in Qatar only. Is the recovery region in Qatar?
We need to check. If not, this arrangement needs a closer look with the QCB before we rely on it.

cards.title: A cheaper cloud provider
