cards.situation: Procurement finds a cloud provider that is 30% cheaper for the bank's customer analytics. The contract would store PII and transaction data in another country, the provider can add sub-contractors without notice, and there is no exit clause. Procurement wants to sign this week.

choices.text: Pause; treat it as a material arrangement, run due diligence, renegotiate sub-contracting notice, audit rights and exit terms, address data location, and seek QCB approval before signing.
choices.outcome: Best. Material arrangements need QCB approval before signing, PII and financial information must be processed in Qatar, and contracts must give notice of sub-contracting, audit rights and an exit plan.

choices.text: Sign now and fix the contract at renewal next year.
choices.outcome: Poor in practice. The bank would already be outside the regulation for a year and remains fully accountable for anything that goes wrong.

choices.text: Sign, but keep only anonymised test data in the cloud until the contract is fixed.
choices.outcome: Partly sensible as risk reduction, but the arrangement still needs the governance steps, and the plan to move live data later must go through due diligence and QCB approval.

cards.title: Dafna Bank's yearly technology risk calendar
cards.caption: An illustrative calendar: the QCB sets the minimum frequencies, the bank chooses the dates.

items.label: Awareness refresh
items.detail: Training content updated; yearly refresher opens for all staff with completion tracking

items.label: Board indicators
items.detail: Cyber indicators reviewed by the board, at least every six months

items.label: Testing
items.detail: Incident response plan test; BCP tests and unplanned drills through the year

items.label: Board indicators
items.detail: Second board review of cyber indicators and remediation plans

items.label: Report and audit
items.detail: Information systems audit; compliance report to the QCB; BCP copy and cloud register to the QCB

cards.title: Real case: keeping banks running during 2022's major events
cards.body:
In its **Financial Stability Review 2022**, the QCB explained that, recognising how important it was for payment systems to keep running during major events, **a business continuity committee was formed** to oversee the continuity of operations of banks and financial institutions.

The review reports that the QCB and the financial sector **continued operations seamlessly** during the event, and presents this as evidence that proactive continuity planning works. The same review lists **managing cyber threats and testing business continuity plans** among the QCB's ongoing efforts to keep payment and settlement systems resilient.

**Why it matters to you:** the drills, simulations and plans in this stage are not paperwork. When demand peaks and the whole country is watching, tested plans are what keep the cards and payments working.

cards.title: Evidence the QCB may ask for
cards.prompt: Match each QCB expectation to the evidence Dafna Bank keeps.

pairs.right: Attendance records, acknowledgements and completion reports
Post-training assessment results and learning scores
Board and senior management session records
Board-signed compliance report and action plans
Test and drill reports, audit findings, BCP copy sent to the QCB
Cloud register, due diligence files and annual assessments

cards.title: Programme check before the QCB visit

cards.front: Is board cyber training on record?
cards.back: Yes: senior management and board members must receive training sessions on cyber threats.
The senior BCM committee owns business continuity communication, training and awareness across the bank.

cards.front: Do incident handlers get extra training?
cards.back: Yes: the cyber crisis plan requires specialised training for personnel handling incidents.
Yes: the data regulation requires training on data security, data protection and privacy.

cards.front: How often is each cloud arrangement assessed?
cards.back: A full assessment of each cloud arrangement every year, including contracts and breaches at the provider.

cards.front: Can the QCB audit at any time?
cards.back: Yes: the QCB may audit the bank's compliance with the Technology Risks Regulation at any point.

cards.question: Under the Cloud Computing Regulation, what must happen before Dafna Bank signs a material cloud arrangement?
options: It must receive official QCB approval
It must publish the contract on its website
It must obtain consent from every shareholder
Nothing beyond the procurement team's sign-off
cards.explanation: The regulation requires official QCB approval before signing any material arrangement or making a material change to an existing one.

cards.title: Stage 5 take-aways
items: A senior head of BCM and a senior committee own continuity, including its training and awareness.
Test plans every year and run at least four unplanned drills, at least one hot and three cold.
The cyber crisis plan covers detection, response, recovery and containment, with specialised training for incident handlers.
Cloud: accountability stays with the bank; keep a register, get QCB approval for material arrangements, test continuity and plan exits.
Keep the evidence: training records, assessments, board sessions, audits, compliance reports and test results.

cards.prompt: If your role were part of tomorrow's unplanned drill, would you know where to go, what to do first and who to call? What is the one thing you would check today?

quiz.question: Under the Technology Risks Regulation, which body is responsible for business continuity communication, training and awareness across the bank?
options: The bank's external auditor
The marketing department alone
Each branch manager acting independently, with no central committee or head office role
A committee of senior officials from IT, HR, legal, business and security
quiz.explanation: Item 6.1.5 makes a committee of senior officials responsible for BCM communication, training and awareness, plan review, budgets, coordination and activation.

quiz.question: Which type of yearly BCP test is described as training personnel in post-incident and crisis management roles?
options: Table-top discussion only
Simulation testing
Component testing of the ATM switch
Supplier SLA testing
quiz.explanation: Simulation testing is the test type used to train personnel in post-incident and crisis management roles. Table-top tests discuss recovery arrangements using example interruptions.

quiz.question: What must the bank send to the QCB each year about business continuity?
options: Nothing unless a crisis has occurred
An approved copy of its BCP with a summary of results
A list of every employee's home address
A copy of each drill's attendance sheet only, without any results or plan document
quiz.explanation: The bank must provide an approved copy of the BCP to the QCB annually, including a summary of results, the status of IT systems and key learnings.

quiz.question: Which four aspects must a cyber crisis management plan include?
options: Detection, response, recovery and containment
Marketing, pricing, sales and service
Hiring, training, appraisal and exit
Budgeting, forecasting, audit and tax
quiz.explanation: The regulation requires the CCMP to cover detection, response, recovery and containment of cyber attacks, with documented roles and procedures.

quiz.question: A payments engineer with highly privileged access asks to work from home permanently. What does the regulation say?
options: Permanent remote work is fine if the engineer uses a personal laptop with antivirus installed
Not for critical functions; privileged users only with prior approval when needed
Remote access is banned for all bank staff in all roles
Remote work is allowed for privileged users without any approval
quiz.explanation: Work-from-home arrangements should not be considered for staff in critical functions; if needed, highly privileged users may connect only with prior approval and as needed.

quiz.question: Dafna Bank's card platform runs on a cloud service. Under the Cloud Computing Regulation, what must the bank do about business continuity?
options: Include the provider in its BCP and tests and document switch-over and back
Remove the platform from the BCP because outsourced services are the provider's responsibility
Rely entirely on the provider's own continuity plan
Test continuity only when the contract is renewed
quiz.explanation: The regulation requires cloud arrangements to be integrated into the BCP, switch-over and switch-back to be detailed in the DR plan and the provider to be included in BCP tests.

quiz.question: How often must a bank disclose its full register of cloud arrangements to the QCB?
options: Every year, and whenever the QCB asks
Every five years
Never; the register is internal only
Only when it changes provider
quiz.explanation: The regulation requires the full register to be disclosed to the QCB annually and on request, alongside the criteria the entity uses to decide materiality.

quiz.question: A manager says, 'Once it is in the cloud, the provider is responsible for compliance.' What does the Cloud Computing Regulation say?
options: Accountability passes to the provider once the contract is signed
Accountability is shared equally by law
The QCB takes over accountability for providers it has approved for use in Qatar
The entity stays fully accountable and cannot delegate it
quiz.explanation: The regulation states that an entity entering into cloud arrangements remains fully accountable for its regulatory obligations and cannot delegate that accountability.

quiz.question: What must a bank's exit plan for a cloud arrangement cover under the regulation?
options: Both a stressed exit and a managed exit
Only a managed exit at contract expiry
Only the provider's own insolvency
Only a price comparison with other providers
quiz.explanation: The regulation requires a documented exit plan covering both stressed and managed exits, with plans to move to another provider or back in-house while keeping continuity.

quiz.question: Which piece of evidence best shows the QCB that Dafna Bank's security awareness training reached everyone?
options: Attendance records with acknowledgements and completion tracking
An email announcing the course dates sent to all branches and departments
A copy of the training slides only
The trainer's invoice for the course
quiz.explanation: The regulation asks banks to keep attendance records and acknowledgements, and suggests monitoring completion. Slides or invoices do not show who was trained.

references.title: Technology Risks Regulation for Banks (January 2018)
references.note: Funded security awareness programme: training at induction, refresher at least yearly including social engineering, content reviewed yearly, assessment after training, attendance and acknowledgement records, and cyber threat training for senior management and the board (2.2.7).

references.title: Technology Risks Regulation for Banks (January 2018)
references.note: Incident framework and owner, central severity setting, all users trained to report incidents (8.2.9), critical incidents reported to the QCB and relevant authorities within 1 hour of identification (8.2.10), yearly testing of the response plan.

references.title: Technology Risks Regulation for Banks (January 2018)
references.note: Board approval of cyber policy, strategy and budget; independent CISO; BCM committee owns BCM training and awareness (6.1.5); yearly BCP testing incl. simulation tests (6.1.9); acceptable use; anti-phishing; fraud prevention training by the fraud team (10.8).

references.title: Data Handling and Protection Regulation
references.note: Data governance unit and Data Privacy Officer; training and awareness on privacy, classification and handling (4.7, 13.2.3); PII, SPI and SFI rules; retention table; customer consent and rights; breaches reported to the QCB, NCSA and Ministry of Interior (section 16).

references.title: Cloud Computing Regulation
references.note: In force from 15 April 2024: cloud strategy, accountability that cannot be delegated, register disclosed to the QCB yearly, due diligence, QCB approval of material arrangements, sub-contracting notice, annual assessment, continuity and exit planning, PII and financial data processed in Qatar.

references.title: Law No. 13 of 2016 - Personal Data Privacy Protection
references.note: Qatar's personal data privacy law, administered by the NCSA; the QCB Data Handling and Protection Regulation requires personal data to be processed in line with it. Not opened: the NCSA page is script-rendered.

references.title: The National Awareness Campaign for Information Security (Stay Aware)
references.note: QCB public campaign with the Ministry of Interior, NCSA and QFCRA naming calls, social media, email, SMS and links as the main fraud channels, with reporting routes for financial cybercrime.

references.title: Financial Stability Review 2022
references.provision: Chapter 4.1.3 (Cyber Security) and the banks' systemic risk survey
references.note: Reports ransomware and phishing as 2022 cyber challenges, the application layer as the most targeted, banks rating cyber risk high, and a business continuity committee for major events.

bank.question: A bank's board wants to approve the cyber security budget but leave the cyber risk appetite to the IT head. What does the Technology Risks Regulation expect?
options: The board approves both the risk appetite and the strategy and budget
Risk appetite is optional if the budget is approved
The QCB sets each bank's risk appetite directly
The IT head sets the risk appetite and the board notes it
bank.explanation: The regulation makes the board responsible for approving the overall cyber risk appetite as well as the cyber security policy, strategy and budget.

bank.question: Which board composition point does the Technology Risks Regulation make about cyber security?
options: The board must exclude anyone with an IT background
Every director must hold a cyber security certificate
The board needs adequate technical representation with cyber experience
The CISO must sit on the board as a voting member with a veto over IT spending
bank.explanation: The regulation asks that the board have adequate technical representation, members with real cyber security experience or expertise, to guide it on cyber matters.

bank.question: Senior management finds a material gap in cyber controls during its yearly adequacy review. What does the regulation expect next?
options: Keep the gap internal until the next QCB inspection, then explain it to the inspectors
Ask the vendor to formally accept the gap
Give the board a reasonable justification for the gap and act on it
Record the gap only if a breach has already happened
bank.explanation: The board asks senior management to review control adequacy at least yearly, and senior management must give the board reasonable justification for any material gaps.

bank.question: Who facilitates the bank's security forum of senior leaders such as the CEO, CFO, CIO and heads of HR, legal and risk?
options: The CISO
The external auditor
The head of marketing
A QCB inspector
bank.explanation: The regulation requires a security forum of senior leaders whose meetings are facilitated by the CISO.

bank.question: Which body reviews the status of the security awareness programme and reports information security activities to the board?
options: The staff social committee
The Information Security Committee
The procurement tender board
The customer complaints unit
bank.explanation: The Information Security Committee's tasks include reviewing the status of the awareness programme, reviewing incidents and reporting to the board on information security.

bank.question: Dafna Bank's compliance report on the Technology Risks Regulation is ready. Who must sign it?
options: The board or a board-authorised committee
The QCB's supervisor for the bank
Any IT team leader
The vendor that supplies the firewall
bank.explanation: The compliance report sent to the QCB must be duly signed by the board or a board-authorised committee, and material gaps are remediated under their guidance.

bank.question: A colleague says the QCB can only check the bank's technology risk compliance through the yearly report. Is that right?
options: No; the QCB may audit the bank's compliance at any time
Yes; the yearly report is the only route, unless the bank asks for a visit itself
No; only the NCSA may audit banks
Yes, unless a critical incident happens
bank.explanation: The regulation states that the QCB reserves the right to audit the bank's compliance with it at any point in time.

bank.question: Which national agency do the QCB rules name, alongside the QCB and the Ministry of Interior, as a recipient of data breach reports?
options: The Qatar Financial Information Unit
The General Tax Authority
The National Cyber Security Agency
The Qatar Stock Exchange
bank.explanation: Section 16 of the data regulation names the National Cyber Security Agency and the Ministry of Interior among the authorised agencies to receive breach reports.

bank.question: Dafna Bank last updated its awareness course content two years ago. Which QCB requirement has it missed?
options: Reviewing and updating training content at least yearly
Translating the course into five languages
Asking customers to approve the content
Running the course only in classrooms
bank.explanation: The regulation requires the content of security training and awareness to be reviewed and updated at least annually for new trends, threats, systems and laws.

bank.question: The bank's head of HR asks whether board members must also take cyber training. What does the Technology Risks Regulation say?
options: Board members are exempt because they approve policy rather than operate systems
Board training is needed only after a breach
Only the board chair needs training
Senior management and board members must get cyber threat training sessions
bank.explanation: Item 2.2.7 requires awareness at all levels and says senior management and board members shall be made aware of the nuances of cyber threats through appropriate training sessions.

bank.question: Which delivery methods does the regulation accept for the yearly awareness training?
options: Only external conferences abroad
Only classroom sessions with a QCB observer
Only printed booklets posted to staff
Computer-based online training or classroom sessions
bank.explanation: The regulation lets the bank choose computer-based online training or classroom-based sessions, as long as completion is mandated and monitored.

bank.question: A branch employee receives an email with an attachment from an unknown sender. Under the acceptable use rules, what should she do?
options: Not open it and report it to the bank's security team
Save it to a USB stick to open at home
Forward it to colleagues to ask their view
Open it on a branch PC to see if it is safe
bank.explanation: The basic security hygiene rules say users should not open attachments from strangers and should report them to the bank's security team.

bank.question: Which customer-facing control does the anti-phishing section expect a bank to offer?
options: An email address where customers can forward suspicious emails
A phone line that reads out customers' passwords on request after basic identity checks
A web page listing customers' account numbers
An app that shares customers' OTPs with partners
bank.explanation: The regulation expects the bank to educate customers about phishing and provide an email address to which customers can forward suspicious emails to check their authenticity.

bank.question: Why does the regulation require a bank to buy domain monitoring services?
options: To measure how many staff read the intranet
To track customers' browsing outside the bank so marketing can target them better
To speed up the bank's website loading times
To spot newly registered look-alike domains used for phishing
bank.explanation: Under anti-phishing, banks must protect their domains and use domain monitoring to flag deceptive registrations similar to their own domains.

bank.question: Fraudulent funds from a scam at another bank land in a Dafna Bank account. The police ask Dafna Bank for documents. What does the regulation expect?
options: Share only if the other bank pays a fee
Share only after the account holder agrees in writing, because of bank secrecy rules
Refuse, because Dafna Bank was not defrauded
Share what the police request, even though Dafna Bank is not the victim
bank.explanation: The regulation says the bank must share data and documents requested by the police even when it is not the victim but has received fraudulent money into its accounts.

bank.question: Which team must itself undergo continuous training to build its skills under the fraud section of the regulation?
options: The facilities management team
The investor relations team
The staff canteen team
The fraud risk management team
bank.explanation: The fraud investigation part says the fraud risk management team must undergo continuous training to enhance its skills and competencies.

bank.question: In the QCB's public 'Stay Aware' campaign, which partners joined the QCB?
options: Only foreign central banks from the region
The General Tax Authority, the QFIU and an airline
The Ministry of Commerce, the stock exchange and a telecom firm
The Ministry of Interior, the NCSA and the QFC Regulatory Authority
bank.explanation: The QCB launched the Stay Aware campaign in cooperation with the Ministry of Interior, the National Cyber Security Agency and the QFC Regulatory Authority.

bank.question: Under the QCB data regulation, whom does the Data Privacy Officer report to?
options: Directly to the CEO or the most senior management position
To the bank's largest shareholder, who chairs the data governance committee
To the head of IT operations
To the marketing director
bank.explanation: The DPO must report directly to the CEO or most senior manager, who makes sure data privacy and protection risks are communicated to the board.

bank.question: A foreign bank's branch in Qatar wants its DPO to sit at headquarters abroad. What does the regulation allow?
options: It may, with no further arrangement in Qatar
It may, but only if the DPO is also the CISO
It may never; the DPO must always live in Qatar and hold Qatari professional qualifications
It may, if a Qatar-based representative liaises to meet the requirements
bank.explanation: A foreign institution may appoint a DPO at its headquarters, provided a Qatar-based representative is responsible for liaising and making sure privacy requirements are consistently met.

bank.question: Which classification rule does the regulation set for sensitive personal information?
options: Classify it only if a customer asks
Leave classification to each branch, based on how often the data is used
Manage it under the highest, most strict classification tier
Treat it like public marketing data
bank.explanation: SPI and SFI must be classified and managed as per the highest, most strict classification available in the institution's framework.

bank.question: How often must the bank at least review its Record of Processing Activities (ROPA), absent major changes?
options: Every ten years with retention
Only when the QCB requests it
Every five years
Every year
bank.explanation: The regulation requires annual ROPA reviews, or reviews triggered by changes such as restructuring, new rules or a changed processing environment.

bank.question: Dafna Bank wants to share customer data with an insurance partner for cross-selling. No legal, regulatory or contractual need applies. What is required first?
options: Only an internal email approval from sales
Nothing, if the partner is licensed in Qatar and signs a confidentiality letter
Customer consent, after explaining the impact of refusing
A notice in a newspaper advertisement
bank.explanation: The bank must collect consent before sharing customer data with a third party unless it is for legal, regulatory or contractual purposes, and must tell customers the impact of not granting consent.

bank.question: A customer asks for a copy of all the personal data Dafna Bank holds about her. In what form must the bank be able to provide it?
options: Only as a handwritten summary by the branch
Only as photographs of the screen
In a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format
Only verbally over the phone
bank.explanation: The regulation requires procedures so customers can access a copy of their data, with information about processing, in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format.

bank.question: Which retention rule applies when another law requires a longer period than the QCB data regulation's minimum?
options: Keep it for the shorter of the two periods
Ask the customer which period to apply
Keep the data for the longer period the other law requires
Delete it at the QCB minimum regardless
bank.explanation: The retention periods are minimums; data must be kept longer where a legal or regulatory mandate requires it, including AML/CFT retention rules.

bank.question: Dafna Bank wants to use a fully autonomous system to approve or reject loan applications with no human review. What does the data regulation require?
options: Only a notice on the bank's website
Nothing, if the model's accuracy has been validated by the bank's own data science team
Only the vendor's written guarantee
QCB approval before processing data in fully autonomous systems
bank.explanation: The regulation requires institutions to assess controls for semi-autonomous or autonomous processing and to seek QCB approval before processing data within fully autonomous decision-making systems.

bank.question: Which regulation items make privacy and data protection training a requirement for employees of QCB-regulated institutions?
options: Items 6.1.8 and 6.1.9 of the Technology Risks Regulation
Items 4.7 and 13.2.3 of the Data Handling and Protection Regulation
Sections 18 and 19 of the Cloud Computing Regulation
Article 1 of Law No. 13 of 2016 only
bank.explanation: Item 4.7 requires training and awareness on privacy, classification and handling, and 13.2.3 requires appropriate training on data security, data protection and privacy. Sections 6.1.8-6.1.9 cover continuity testing.

bank.question: Who owns and manages the incident management programme, including its budget, under the Technology Risks Regulation?
options: Whoever reports the incident first, until the incident is closed by the help desk
A person the bank appoints, who is also the security contact point
The bank's external legal counsel
The QCB's on-call supervisor
bank.explanation: The bank must appoint a person who owns and manages the incident management programme, including budget and execution, and acts as the contact point for information security communications.

bank.question: Besides cyber incidents, what does the regulation say users should be trained to respond to as part of incident management?
options: Certain incidents such as fire and natural disasters
Media questions about share prices
Customer complaints about pricing
Disputes over staff bonuses
bank.explanation: Item 8.2.9 says all users must be trained to report incidents to the incident team and to respond to certain incidents, such as fire or natural disasters.

bank.question: After a major incident causing severe disruption, which items must the root cause analysis include under the regulation?
options: Only the name of the employee to blame and the disciplinary action taken against them
Only the vendor's invoice for the fix
Only the number of emails sent during the incident
Timeline, losses, customers affected, reputation and corrective actions
bank.explanation: The regulation lists timelines, revenue loss, costs, customers affected, implications for reputation and confidence, and corrective and preventive measures.

bank.question: A large-scale cyber attack hits several Gulf banks. What does the regulation expect Dafna Bank to do even if it is only lightly affected?
options: Inform only its own shareholders
Stay silent so competitors and customers do not learn about the bank's exposure
Keep the QCB and the Ministry of Interior informed
Wait for the QCB to ask before saying anything
bank.explanation: Item 8.2.14 asks banks to keep the QCB and MOI informed of incidents such as large-scale cyber incidents, so that proactive measures can reduce risk to the financial sector.

bank.question: An incident ticket was raised as 'low' by a branch, but the central team sees signs of a wider attack. What should happen?
options: The ticket is closed and a new one opened next week once the branch has more facts
The vendor decides the final rating
The central team re-classifies it and applies the matching escalation
The branch rating stands because it was first
bank.explanation: Severity is set by the centralised incident response team, with escalation and resolution matched to the severity. If it becomes critical, the 1-hour reporting rule applies from identification.

bank.question: Which definition matches a 'data breach' in the QCB data regulation?
options: A planned upgrade of the core banking system
Protected data accessed, disclosed or stolen by unauthorised people
Any delay in answering a customer's email
An authorised transfer of customer data to the QCB in response to a supervisory request
bank.explanation: A data breach is an incident where sensitive, confidential or protected data is accessed, disclosed or stolen by unauthorised individuals. Misuse by authorised users is a data privacy breach.

bank.question: A breach exposes customers' card data. Under section 16, which action fits the duty to trigger action by stakeholders?
options: Waiting until fraud losses appear before telling anyone, to avoid unnecessary alarm
Alerting affected customers and staff so cards can be blocked
Asking customers to sign that the bank is not liable
Removing the incident from the internal log
bank.explanation: Section 16 requires the institution to trigger action from relevant stakeholders, including employees and customers, to circumvent the potential impact of the breach.

bank.question: Which customer reporting route for financial cybercrime does the QCB's Stay Aware campaign mention?
options: The QCB's exchange rate service
The Ministry of Interior's Metrash2 application
A post on the bank's social media page
The bank's annual general meeting
bank.explanation: The Stay Aware page tells the public to report financial cybercrime through a Ministry of Interior hotline, the Metrash2 app or email.

bank.question: In a hot test under the regulation's unplanned drill requirement, what happens?
options: Only one server is restarted in the data centre while staff stay at their usual desks
The bank checks that fire alarms ring
Activities move from the original site to the alternate site in full
Managers discuss a scenario around a table
bank.explanation: The hot test is a full simulation in which activities are relocated from the original site to the alternative site; cold tests cover selected components.

bank.question: Who must assess the effectiveness of the bank's BCP testing programme and report to the Audit Committee?
options: The head of marketing
Internal audit, with an independent external audit also each year
The vendor that hosts the recovery site
The customer complaints unit
bank.explanation: Internal audit assesses the testing programme, reviews results and reports to the Audit Committee, and an independent experienced external auditor reviews it annually.

bank.question: Which standard does the regulation give as an example to align the bank's BCM policy, procedures and plans with?
options: ISO 9001
IFRS 9
bank.explanation: The regulation says BCM policies, procedures and plans should follow a global standard such as ISO 22301, alongside the QCB's business continuity instructions.

bank.question: Under the Cloud Computing Regulation, where must PII and financial information processed in a cloud arrangement be processed?
options: Within Qatar only
Wherever the provider's prices are lowest
In any country with a privacy law
Anywhere in the GCC without approval
bank.explanation: The regulation requires entities to ensure that PII and financial information is processed within Qatar only, consistent with the data regulation's location rules.

bank.question: A cloud provider plans to add a new sub-contractor that will process Dafna Bank's data. What must the arrangement give the bank?
options: A discount on fees but no say in the change
Notice in time to assess the risk, and the right to object
Notice after the change, for information only
No notice, because sub-contracting is the provider's own business and outside the contract
bank.explanation: Where sub-contracting is allowed, the CSP must notify the entity in time for a risk assessment, and the entity must be able to object or give explicit approval.

bank.question: How often must a QCB-regulated entity carry out a full assessment of each cloud arrangement?
options: Every five years
Every year
Only at contract signing
Only after a provider breach
bank.explanation: The regulation requires a full annual assessment of each cloud arrangement, covering contracts, failures, breaches at the provider and location changes.

bank.question: When contracting a cloud provider, what must the bank's contract say about incidents at the provider?
options: The provider reports incidents only at year end
The provider reports incidents affecting the bank without undue delay
The provider may keep incidents confidential from the bank if it fixes them within a week
The provider reports incidents only to its own board
bank.explanation: Material arrangement contracts must oblige the provider to report incidents that affected the entity's operation or service without undue delay.

bank.question: Ahmed, the board risk committee chair, asks for one item that proves the board itself met its QCB cyber training duty. Which is best?
options: Staff completion rates for the yearly refresher only, broken down by department and branch
Records of cyber threat sessions held for the board and senior management
The CISO's own professional certificates
A copy of the cloud provider's ISO certificate
bank.explanation: Item 2.2.7 requires senior management and board members to be made aware of cyber threats through training sessions, so session records are the direct evidence. Staff completion rates cover a different duty.
